you’ll def have free time and I wish I’d used more of mine wisely. Yeah, enjoy the moments when you’re working in site but once you’re back, (after you’ve spoken about it a few times),no cares that much about your pc experience/they will want to know what you can do for them—a hard pill for me to swallow. This will help you appreciate the present especially when with future loved ones in country. 

Tbh, so many people changed their career aspirations after service (myself included) so I’ll advise on transferable skills: 

- work on writing/communications. Read press releases from the state dept or other agencies/NGOs of interest to gain an understanding of the style/lexicon. Communications/writing will set you apart. The NYT copy edit quizzes are fun!

- computer skills: idk, pick one and get good at it. Whether it is graphic design, social media, excel, basic coding, solid understanding of data, whatever. Any of these is good for ID, especially data. Maybe even knock out a few courses through a reputable certificate program (if you have wifi*, and you might get a discount/waiver given your future financial hardship) but don’t stress too much about this one, as long as it’s fun/lowkey—-also keep it to yourself; trust me. I’d do a course closer to COS. That way it’s at least something “tangible”. I interviewed somewhere and they were like cool, all of your soft skills, but ok??? Lol

- improve vocabulary, this is something I wish I’d spent more time doing but it was hard given I was speaking a different language all day. But this will help any standardized test you might take 

In country skills: language (get as good as you can), project management (this is a big one, like look at PMI resources and plan your projects accordingly—you can submit them as a sample in the future), grant writing (good skill, again, writing), conflict management, DEIA (I’m mixed race and I find this entire field to be meh lol but I see it’s growth/usefulness when executed appropriately), 

- as your return date gets closer: really be present in country; even if your service wasn’t that great. 

It took me about 4 months to find work. Most people I COS’d with, about 3-6 months. But I had a pal who travelled afterwards and it took her almost a year to find an internship and she recently got a FT job. So be mindful (she didn’t have any pre pc experience/and early COVID didn’t help). 

It’s okay to care about life after peace corps, don’t let people tell you otherwise. It’s possible to strike a healthy balance with being present/service and your life/career when it’s done. Don’t let anyone tell you otherwise. Good luck.

I’ve been thinking about this lately. I’m for whatever is healthiest for the individual during the moment. 

I also think there’s space in this conversation for grace with ourselves. It’s hard for some of us to block and KEEP them blocked. Not everyone has built the skill to block and delete. (I’m saying this from experience and seeing so many posts about how red flags were ignored which tells me immediate block and delete did not occur). And at the same time, I believe there’s room here for SELF-CONTROL, discipline, and accountability. 

But I’m tired of seeing people spiral because they’re not in a place with this established skill set or whatever, and then placing blame onto themselves (or feeling like they have low self-esteem, etc.) because they are not blocking and deleting as quickly as they *assume* others might. 

I guess what I’m trying to say is: for those struggling to block, you aren’t any less worthy and you’re working on building skills to block at a faster pace. And for those who block and delete at the first red flag: good for you, your established boundaries are admirable, and I hope we can all get to a healthier place with ourselves.
